content.comment: We thank the reviewers for their comments. While we already worked on most of the discussed issues before the reviews were released to explain the contribution and results better, we do not believe we can convince 3 people to change their score. We therefore choose to withdraw. Thanks again for the helpful comments.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a unified framework that tackles the problem of room layout estimation from multi-view panoramas. The solution consists of (1) a GRP-Net that predicts the layout boundary correspondences and horizon-ceiling/floor coordinates, and (2) a registration module that estimates the relative camera pose from predicted corresdpondences. Then final reconstruction is obtained by fusing the induvidual layouts with the help of estimated relative pose. This method achieves a new SOTA which demonstrates the effectiveness of the solution in regarding to panorama registration and reconstruction.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:\
(1) As noted by the author as "geometry-aware", geometry is enforced into the solution. As a result, it achieves better performance than pose regression (e.g. PSMNet);\
(2) This paper is well written, and the experiments are also sufficiently explained.\
Weakness:\
From my perspective, the major weeakness is the technical novelty. Reducing pose estimation to finding point/feature correspodences is well  known,and the performance improvement is also expected. The idea of GPR-Net seems to be applying COTR to the special case of paranoma reconstruction. To be more specific, the general architecture of GPR-Net and the loss functions are same with COTR. The representations of paranoma are already used in LED$^2$-Net. Therefore, I think it is a good solution, but does not provide enough new insights.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
(1) This paper is easy to read and follow. The idea, equations and the experiments are expalined well.\
(2) The quality is good. It has a clean solution with enough experiments that can prove its effectiveness. \
(3) I think the novelty of this paper is only marginal. Please refer to the "Weakness" part above for details.\
(4) Although the authors did not promise to release the code, I think the idea of this paper is reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: My only conern is the novelty of this work. If the authors can clarify more about this part, I would like to raise my rating.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a novel method / way to address the room layout estimation with cuboid assumptions as a multi-view, wide baseline registration of 360° panoramas. The resulting conceptual method is dubbed GPR-Net (Geometry-aware Panorama Registration Network) and builds upon a very recent published work from CVPR 2022 which focused on layout merging from a pair of 360° panoramas
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
** Strengths

- (1) Readability.
Overall, the readability is on point. The main ideas are well conveyed, justified and articulated while mostly providing sufficient context to the reader, albeit sometimes superficially (cf. below for the downsides). The grammar, and overall the writing, is relatively mature in its current state.


- (2) Experimental Evaluation.
Despite a few ambiguities and conceptual issues (as discussed below), the main ingredients are present and mostly well executed. It can still be seen as a mixed bag until we address the negative aspects in the reviewers/authors discussion to sort this one out.

- (3) The Organization and Structure of the Contents.

Most sections are well balanced, structured and populated. The Related Work discussion in particular is populated by the main references in the field and are accurately discussed and put in perspective.

- (4) The Quality of the Visual Depictions and Illustrations.

This applies to the conveyed information as well as in terms of their esthetics, the qualitative depictions and illustrations are very well made throughout.

** Weaknesses:

- (1) Is the experimental comparison performed in a fair setup?

Regarding Table 1 and the reported comparison with PSMNet (CVPR 2022), the corresponding performance comes from the original paper but there seem to lack a few layers of details here to help assess whether the comparative setup is fair and comparable.

For example, only the overall IoUs are given rather than per-overlap splits (low, medium, high). Similarly, there must be a thorought discussion on this table / aspect in particular.

- (2) The practical usability of the proposed framework.

The main conceptual proposition of the submitted paper builds upon existing PSMNet (CVPR 2022) and revamps the network to an increasingly more complex one with an online RANSAC pose estimation / refinement .

- (3) Terminology is key.

While the method is sold as a "Multi-View" revisit of an existing paper, it only addresses and evaluates in a stereo setup. It is hence slightly misleading to sell it as Multi-View vs. stereo as other existing work do.

- (4) Registration Comparisons wrt State-of-the-art could be more pertinent, up to date, informative and compelling.

OpenMVG (Moulon 2016) is a reasonable baseline but alternative and more recent SfM pipelines are available and as easy to use and are notoriously better on public benchmarks in multiples scenario. To only cite one, please refer to the following:

* KNAPITSCH, Arno, PARK, Jaesik, ZHOU, Qian-Yi, et al. Tanks and temples: Benchmarking large-scale scene reconstruction. ACM Transactions on Graphics (ToG), 2017.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
As stated above in the review, the clarity, quality and reproducibility aspects are mostly on point. The reproducibility comes with a relatvie caveat, but remains reasonable regarding the standards in the field.

The main problem is with regards to the experimental reproducibility of Table 1 wrt the CVPR 2022 baseline.
content.summary_of_the_review:
While there are numerous potential positives to this one, there is one avenue for ambiguity regarding the experimental setup which must definitely be addresses explicitely and without any remaining gray area post-discussion. 

Additionally, I am having a hard time buying the practical usability or even usefulness of the proposed pipeline which already builds upon a complex existing piece, and adds a RANSAC-based component which is ad hoc wrt the rest of the Neural Network architecture.

Performance aside, this is tough to deal with in practice and the ad-hoc aspect makes it look like a transitional incremental contirbution.

I could still revisit my stance after discussing the experimental setup, the missing bits of information and would be very happy to do so.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a method to reconstruct 3D layouts from a set of 360 panoramas. Prior works have addressed this topic, but most, like the current state of the art (Wang et al., 2022), require having reasonable pose estimates to start from. Obtaining those initial estimates typically requires an external process, such as structure-from-motion, odometry, or SLAM. The proposed method removes the need for initial pose estimates as a prior. Instead, it jointly learns how to register the panoramas while also predicting the 3D layout of the room, doing so in an end-to-end fashion. In particular, the method is described to be particularly effective at wide baseline panorama registration.

Experiments are performed on the large-scale Zillow Indoor Dataset (Cruz et al., 2021), and the results demonstrate improvements over the prior state of the art in both panorama registration performance and layout estimation according to standard metrics. Both quantitative and qualitative analyses are present.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

* This paper demonstrates significant improvement in standard benchmark metrics for layout estimate accuracy without the need for external camera registration. Removing this additional step is important, especially for indoor scenes and panoramic imagery, as both the presence of large homogeneous surfaces and spherical image distortion are frequent failure cases for traditional camera registration.


**Weaknesses**

* This paper only evaluates results on a single dataset: Zillow Indoor (Cruz et al., 2021). It would be more convincing to see that the improvements hold across other indoor layout datasets, such as PanoContext (Zhang et al., 2014). Moreover, given that an important aspect of this work is the ability to register cameras from scratch, demonstrating generalizability would be helpful. SfM and SLAM systems generalize across scenes by design (they optimize to a specific set of data). To take the camera registration contribution seriously requires some signal that it generalizes across datasets.

* Table 4 provides somewhat counterintuitive results. Why would sampling fewer rays provide increased layout reconstruction accuracy? This is an especially interesting outcome when evaluating layout IoU. One might expect that a higher ray sampling would lead to a less course layout estimate. The results suggest otherwise, however. More discussion of this effect is deserved in Section 4.4.

* It would be useful to understand the robustness to pose errors in registration. Tables 4 and 5 indicate that experiments on layout accuracy were done with GT poses as well as with estimated poses, and generally estimated poses do see accuracy drop a bit. It would benefit the paper to include a discussion as to whether there is a direct relationship between average pose error and layout accuracy. A manufactured experiment of jittering the poses with increasing noise could help to illustrate this. If concerned that such a test would be unrealistic in terms of pose error distribution, a plot of layout accuracy against pose error for all scenes in the test set could help illustrate if such a relationship exists.

**Other Questions/Suggestions**
* The paper mentions that OpenMVG fails on 76% of panorama pairs, and therefore the assumption of externally compute poses is not always possible due to wide baselines. This is a fair point, but the fact that the paper earlier brings up Shabani et al. (2021), which is a ultra-wide baseline registration method, invites the question of how well it performs. How does Shabani et al. (2021) fair when registering test set panoramas?

* It might be helpful to show some examples of where GPR-Net successfully registered the panoramas but OpenMVG failed. It could be especially enlightening if performance were broken down by percentage of FOV overlap.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Quality**

The paper presents a well-motivated method and performs sufficient experiments to justify its claims. In general, the quality of the research is good. The experimental benchmarks are recent and relevant papers that approach the same problem in a different way, and the metrics used for evaluation are effective to demonstrate relative performance. The paper also offers ablation experiments that mostly support the design choices (see question about Table 4) and also justify the claims about the network's ability to jointly optimize poses and layouts (Table 5).

One type of ablation study is missing that could be helpful: evaluating predictions of correspondences, overlaps, and floor/ceiling coordinates without the other output heads. While all the prediction components are ultimately used together to produce the resulting layouts, it would be helpful to understand to what extent the different tasks support each other's performance.

**Clarity**

The paper on the whole is organized and well-written when discussing the problem and the experimental results. There are a few areas, nevertheless, that could be improved for clarity. Most notably, these issues arise in the descriptions of the methodology.

One example of this is the explanation of the network. Despite Figure 2 and the explanation in Section 3.1, the network architecture is not abundantly clear. Specifically hard to follow is how rays are sampled from the panorama at original resolution, positionally encoded, and then associated with the downscaled feature map's tokens in the transformer. My understanding is that each line of latitude in the original panorama is converted to query rays and associated with the complete embedded feature map before being fed into the relevant MLP head. However, after a few reads, I am still not clear on this. For reproducibility, it would be beneficial for the authors to better clarify the network architecture description.

The other aspect that could be made clearer is the description of the nonlinear registration in Section 3.3. Figure 3 is not particularly helpful. It is not clear what the boundary point sets represent or how they relate to either the panoramas or the layout. It is not well explained why $\mathbb{U}^2$ is not necessarily a uniform distribution. Is this due to the nonlinear distortion of the panorama, the fact that the pair of panoramas may not share significant fields of view, or something else entirely?

*Questions*

The paper refers multiple times to a "global pixel-space registration", which is a phrasing I am unfamiliar with. It would help the paper to more clearly define what this phrase is referring to. It seems to mean registration performed by identifying correspondences in pixels (e.g. SIFT feature matching followed by epipolar modeling) Is that understanding correct?

**Originality**

This paper builds on aspects of some prior work, using attention as in PSMNet (Wang et al., 2022), transformers as in (Jiang et al, 2022), a cycle-consistency loss (Jiang et al., 2021), and the layout-to-depth transform (Wang et al., 2021). It also adds new concepts to the mix, most notable a different architecture that uses positionally-encoded horizon lines as queries, and the correspondence map prediction, which enables the joint camera registration process.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I am on the fence about acceptance to ICLR. The focus on a single dataset and the clarity concerns in the methodology explanation are my primary concerns. The experimental results suggest that the proposed methodology is an improvement on existing work. Moreover, the ability to jointly optimize both the poses and layouts is theoretically a boon, as model training should be able to help enforce geometric consistency. The paper is held back due to generalizability concerns and clarity issues though. If the method explanation is unclear, it is fair to question how this work can provide new insight to other researchers.

It would be helpful for the authors to address both generalizability and clarity in their rebuttal. This appears to be a nice paper with convincing results, but I am having a hard time understanding the method as described. If those issues can be resolved, I believe this paper's publication would benefit other researchers working on this topic.

content.title: GPR-Net: Multi-view Layout Estimation via a Geometry-aware Panorama Registration Network
content.abstract: Reconstructing 3D layouts from multiple $360^{\circ}$ panoramas has received increasing attention recently as estimating a complete layout of a large-scale and complex room from a single panorama is very difficult. A state-of-the-art method, called PSMNet, introduces the first learning-based framework that jointly estimates the room layout and registration given a pair of panoramas. However, PSMNet relies on an approximate (i.e., "noisy") registration as input. This assumption is inherently a challenging problem in the context of wide baseline registration. In this work, we present a complete multi-view panoramic layout estimation framework that jointly learns panorama registration and layout estimation given a pair of panoramas without relying on a pose prior. The major improvement over PSMNet comes from a novel Geometry-aware Panorama Registration Network or GPR-Net that effectively tackles the wide baseline registration problem by exploiting the layout geometry and computing fine-grained correspondences on the layout boundaries, rather on the global pixel-space. Our architecture consists of two parts. First, given two panoramas, we adopt a vision transformer to learn a set of compact 1D horizon features sampled on the panorama. These 1D horizon features encode the depths of individual layouts and the correspondence and covisibility maps between layout boundaries. We then exploit a non-linear registration module to convert these 1D horizon features into a set of corresponding 2D boundary points on the layout. Finally, we estimate the final relative camera pose via RANSAC and obtain the complete layout simply by taking the union of registered layouts. Experimental results indicate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both panorama registration and layout estimation on a large-scale indoor panorama dataset.
